extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and students of poetry; literary readers and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the principles, style, and aesthetic criteria that define good poetry (especially lyric and short poems), including rhythm, imagery, tone, and the relation of poetry to truth and morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue brevity / Length
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem may be improperly brief. Undue brevity degenerates into mere epigrammatism; a very short poem, while now and then producing a brilliant or vivid effect, never produces a profound or enduring effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be the steady pressing down of the stamp upon the wax — sustained development to create depth. Examples given: Shelley’s short serenade is exquisite but not widely familiar; many brief works have been kept back from their proper position by undue brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem per se (art for art's sake)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem written simply for the poem’s sake — 'this poem per se' — is thoroughly dignified and supremely noble; the poem as poem can be the ultimate object of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the notion that every poem must inculcate a moral truth; the poem’s province is Beauty. The true artist may write for the poem itself without apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-didacticism / relation to Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that the ultimate object of all Poetry is Truth is false; Truth’s modes of inculcation differ radically from the poetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When enforcing truth, prefer severity rather than efflorescence of language: be simple, precise, terse, cool, calm, unimpassioned. Truth can be introduced incidentally, but the true artist will tone such truth down in subjection to Beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as sole arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's sole arbiter is Taste; Intellect and Conscience have only collateral relations with the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems by their relation to the Beautiful (inclusive of the sublime), rather than by conformity to Reason or Morality; Taste assesses harmony, proportion, and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and musicality (metre, rhythm, rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Music — in its various modes of metre, rhythm, and rhyme — is of so vast a moment in Poetry as never to be wisely rejected; it is a vitally important adjunct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The union of Poetry with Music often brings the soul nearest to supernal Beauty. Historical examples: old bards and minnesingers, Thomas Moore singing his own songs; do not decline musical assistance in verse when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural manner / ease of tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural manner or 'ease' in literary style is not merely appearance; it is the result of writing with understanding and adopting the tone most people would adopt for the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ease should match occasion; being uniformly 'quiet' or uniform in manner is artificial and often silly. The 'insouciance' of Longfellow’s metre is praised as matching sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Sentiment: elevation distinct from passion and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poetic Sentiment is the human aspiration for supernal Beauty and produces an elevating excitement of the soul, distinct from Passion (the intoxication of the heart) and Truth (satisfaction of the Reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sentiment often carries a 'taint' of sadness or longing (a pleasurable sadness). The poet aims to suggest the 'Beauty above' rather than merely describe beauty before us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Passion and Truth (subordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion tends to degrade rather than elevate the soul; truth and duty may be introduced but only incidentally and subordinated to Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor themes and treatments that elevate. Love — especially the 'true, the divine Eros' — is singled out as the purest and truest poetic theme. Tone down passionate or didactic elements so they serve the poetic atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery that suggests the supernal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic effect is induced by suggestive images and sensations — sights, sounds, odors, colors, and sentiments that point beyond the merely earthly toward a higher loveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evocative elements (examples from text): star-orbs, flowers, waving grain-fields, distant mountains, clouds, brooks, silver rivers, sequestered lakes, night-wind, perfume, exotic odours from distant islands, music, noble thoughts, chivalrous deeds, and the beauty of woman — all as means to hint at supernal Beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained emotional impact ('pressing down of the stamp')
rubrics_metrics.description: For profundity and endurance, a poem must produce a sustained impression rather than a fleeting sparkle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid poems that are no more than 'feathers of fancy' blown aloft; work toward depth that 'stamps' itself upon the reader’s attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of versification to theme and mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Versification (meter, rhythm, fancifulness) must be adapted to the poem’s subject and mood — even when bordering on the fanciful, it should serve the thematic thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Bridge of Sighs' uses fanciful versification adapted to the poem’s wild insanity; Byron’s difficult rhythm suits his subject. Choose forms and rhythms that amplify theme and affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic’s duty: avoid over-asserting merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing out too particularly the merits of a work of art is to admit they are not self-evident; excellence should be self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Apollo/Zoilus anecdote warns critics: excessive cataloguing of beauties implies they are not plainly apparent. Let true excellence speak for itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of Fancy and Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy and Imagination are distinct faculties; a poet may be fanciful without lacking deep imagination — fancy can dominantly shape a poet’s work to great effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake predominance of fancy for absence of imagination (example: Thomas Moore). Recognize and value the imaginative power present within fanciful works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: True poetic lines often breathe an earnestness and sincerity of sentiment; earnest tone contributes to poetic elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Willis’s poem is praised for sincere earnestness and energy as opposed to mere 'verses of society.' Hyperbole can be pardoned if earnest enthusiasm underlies it (example: Pinckney).
